item.title: The Count
item.description: The lining of your gut replaces itself every three to five days. The outer layer of your skin turns over every few weeks. Red blood cells last about four months. These are the fast parts. Fat cells turn over at roughly ten percent per year. Heart muscle cells renew more slowly. Cortical neurons don't turn over at all. You are a mosaic of layers at different ages.

item.title: The Record That Isn't For It
item.description: The bomb pulse in the shark lens. The record is not information for the shark — there is no mechanism by which the animal uses this. The archive is inside it; it's not for it. The longest-lasting records are often ones that formed as a side effect and were never destroyed. The stable ones are the passive ones.

item.title: What Doesn't Turn Over
item.description: The Greenland shark lives 400+ years. Its eye lens crystalline proteins form before birth and are never replaced — a chemical record of the moment of formation, unmodified across centuries. The bomb pulse from 1950s-60s nuclear testing left a C-14 spike in the lenses of sharks born after 1963. The archive is inside the animal. It's not for it.

item.title: Two Scales
item.description: The temporal order judgment threshold (~30ms) is the grain of temporal experience: the smallest detectable interval. The specious present (~3000ms) is the window: how far back now extends. A 3-second window contains roughly 100 grains. Both are measured from behavior. Neither is accessible from inside.

item.title: No Knife-Edge
item.description: Poets across eight languages landed at the same line duration: 2.5 to 3.5 seconds. So did the Necker cube switching period, speech phrases, and musical phrases. The brain has a fixed integration window — and the philosopher who named it called it specious, meaning deceptive.

item.title: Before B Arrived
item.description: Flash A is blue, flash B is orange. In the motion zone, the moving dot changes color mid-trajectory — before B has appeared. The brain has drawn on information from an event that hasn't happened yet at the moment the color change is experienced.

item.title: The Green S
item.description: Building the phoneme restoration simulation required showing the generated phoneme — green, visible, marked. But that’s the experimenter’s perspective. The subject has no such mark.

item.title: Where the Cough Was
item.description: Warren replaced a phoneme in a recording with a cough. Subjects heard nothing missing — and when asked to locate the cough, they couldn't. The generation erases its own location.

item.title: The Commitment
item.description: Built bistable.html: Necker cube and Rubin's vase. The interesting thing isn't that the brain flips between interpretations of an ambiguous figure — it's that it commits exclusively to one at a time.
